title: Definition
body_md:
A weak solution $u$ of \eqref{eq:sing}, respectively \eqref{eq:exp}, is \emph{stable outside a closed set} $K\subset\mathbb{R}^N$ if
\[
Q_u(\varphi)\ge q\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}u^{-q-1}\varphi^2,\qquad\text{respectively}\qquad Q_u(\varphi)\ge\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}e^u\varphi^2,
\]
for every $\varphi\in C^1_c(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K)$. It is \emph{stable} if this holds with $K=\emptyset$. Its \emph{Morse index} is the supremum of the dimensions of subspaces of $C^1_c(\mathbb{R}^N)$ on which the corresponding quadratic form
\[
\mathcal Q_u^{\rm sing}(\varphi):=Q_u(\varphi)-q\int u^{-q-1}\varphi^2,
\qquad
\mathcal Q_u^{\rm exp}(\varphi):=Q_u(\varphi)-\int e^u\varphi^2
\]
is negative definite. Thus a stable solution has Morse index zero. The index may also be infinite.

label: thm:exterior
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:exterior}
Assume that $(H)$ holds and $p\ge2$. Let $R_0\ge0$ and $E:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:H_0(x)>R_0\}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let $q>0$ and $N>q\tau$. If $u\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}(E)\cap C(E)$ is a positive weak solution of $\Delta_p^Hu=u^{-q}$ in $E$, then
\[
\liminf_{r\to\infty}\ r^{-\tau}\min_{\{H_0=r\}}u\ \le\ c_s .
\]
\item Let $N>p$. If $u\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}(E)\cap C(E)$ is a weak solution of $-\Delta_p^Hu=e^u$ in $E$, then
\[
\limsup_{r\to\infty}\ r^{p}\max_{\{H_0=r\}}e^u\ \ge\ p^{p-1}(N-p) .
\]
\end{enumerate}
Both inequalities become equalities for $U_q$ and $U_e$.

label: thm:outside
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:outside}
Assume that $(H)$ holds and $p\ge2$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item If $p\le N<\frac{p(p+3)}{p-1}$ and $q>q_c(N,p)$, then $\Delta_p^Hu=u^{-q}$ has no positive weak solution in $\mathbb{R}^N$ that is stable outside a compact set.
\item If $p<N<\frac{p(p+3)}{p-1}$, then $-\Delta_p^Hu=e^u$ has no weak solution in $\mathbb{R}^N$ that is stable outside a compact set.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, in these ranges neither equation has a solution of finite Morse index.

label: thm:Nliouville
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:Nliouville}
Assume that $(H)$ holds and $N\ge2$. A weak solution of $-\Delta_N^Hu=e^u$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ is stable outside a compact set if and only if it is one of the functions \eqref{eq:bubbles}. In particular, every solution of finite Morse index is one of these functions.

label: thm:sharp
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:sharp}
Assume that $(H)$ holds and $p\ge2$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let $N\ge p$ and $q>0$. For every $a>0$ the equation $\Delta_p^Hu=u^{-q}$ has a unique positive solution $u_a\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^N)$ of the form $u_a(x)=v(H_0(x))$ with $u_a(0)=a$. If either $N>p$ or $N=p>2$, and $q\le q_c(N,p)$, in particular if $N\ge\frac{p(p+3)}{p-1}$, then $u_a$ is stable. In these cases $u_a(x)>U_q(x)$ for every $x\ne0$.
\item Let $N>p$. The function $U_e$ belongs to $W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and is a weak solution of $-\Delta_p^Hu=e^u$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$. It is stable if and only if $N\ge\frac{p(p+3)}{p-1}$.
\item Let $N=p>2$ and $q>0$. The function $U_q$ belongs to $W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N)$ and is a weak solution of $\Delta_p^Hu=u^{-q}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$, positive except at the origin. It is stable if and only if $q\le\frac{(p-2)^2}4$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
If $p=2$ and $\alpha=-1$, both exponents on the right equal $2$ and $m\ge1$. The stability inequality with $\varphi=\eta^m$ and \eqref{eq:Mbound} give $q\int u^{-q-1}\eta^{2m}\le C\int m^2\eta^{2m-2}|\nabla\eta|^2\le C\int|\nabla\eta|^2$, which is \eqref{eq:est_sing}. So let $\alpha\ne-1$. Then $\alpha<-1$, and we use
\[
\mu:=\frac{(\alpha+1)^2}{4|\alpha|},\qquad \theta_1:=\frac{-1-\alpha}{q-\alpha},\qquad \theta_2:=\frac{1-p-\alpha}{q-\alpha}.
\]
Both $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ lie in $[0,1)$.

The choice of $\alpha$ gives $\lambda\mu<q$. Indeed, with $s=|\alpha|$, the inequality $\lambda(\alpha+1)^2<4q|\alpha|$ reads $\lambda s^2-2(\lambda+2q)s+\lambda<0$, that is, $s_-<s<s_+$, where $s_\pm$ are the roots. Since $s_+=-\alpha_0$ and $s_-s_+=1$, we have $s_-<1<s$ and $s<s_+$.

For $k\in\mathbb{N}$, let $a_k$ and $b_k$ be equal to $t^{\frac{\alpha+1}2}$ and $t^\alpha$ for $t\ge\frac1k$, and to their tangent lines at $t=\frac1k$ for $0<t<\frac1k$:
\[
a_k(t)=k^{-\frac{\alpha+1}2}+\tfrac{\alpha+1}2k^{\frac{1-\alpha}2}\big(t-\tfrac1k\big),\qquad
b_k(t)=k^{-\alpha}+\alpha k^{1-\alpha}\big(t-\tfrac1k\big)\qquad(0<t<\tfrac1k).
\]
These functions are positive, decreasing, of class $C^1$, bounded with bounded derivatives, and $a_k'^2=\mu|b_k'|$. A direct computation gives
\[
a_k(t)^2-tb_k(t)=\frac{(\alpha-1)^2}{4k^{\alpha+1}}(1-kt)^2\qquad\text{for }0<t<\tfrac1k,
\]
and $a_k^2=tb_k$ for $t\ge\frac1k$. Hence $t^{-q}b_k\le t^{-q-1}a_k^2=q^{-1}g'a_k^2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:key} applies with $\nu=q$. Put $F_k(t):=t^{-q-1}a_k(t)^2$ and let $\Phi_k$ and $\Psi_k$ be the functions $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:key} for $a_k,b_k$. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trunc_sing}
\Phi_k\le C F_k^{\theta_1},\qquad \Psi_k\le CF_k^{\theta_2}\qquad\text{on }(0,\infty),
\end{equation}
with $C=C(p,q,\alpha)$. For $t\ge\frac1k$, $F_k(t)=t^{\alpha-q}$, $\Phi_k(t)=(1+|\alpha|^{-1})t^{\alpha+1}$, and $\Psi_k(t)=\big((\frac{|\alpha+1|}2)^{2-p}+|\alpha|^{1-p}\big)t^{\alpha+p-1}$, while $(\alpha-q)\theta_1=\alpha+1$ and $(\alpha-q)\theta_2=\alpha+p-1$. For $0<t<\frac1k$, the bounds $k^{-\frac{\alpha+1}2}\le a_k\le\frac{1-\alpha}2k^{-\frac{\alpha+1}2}$, $b_k\le(1-\alpha)k^{-\alpha}$, $|a_k'|=\frac{|\alpha+1|}2k^{\frac{1-\alpha}2}$, and $|b_k'|=|\alpha|k^{1-\alpha}$ give $F_k\ge k^{q-\alpha}$, $\Phi_k\le Ck^{-1-\alpha}$, and $\Psi_k\le Ck^{1-p-\alpha}$, which is \eqref{eq:trunc_sing}.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:key} with $\psi=\eta^m$. Note that $m\ge1$ by \eqref{eq:m_sing}, since $q-\alpha\ge q+p-1$. By \eqref{eq:trunc_sing} and Young's inequality with exponents $\frac1{\theta_i}$ and $\frac1{1-\theta_i}$,
\begin{align*}
Cm^2\Phi_k(u)\eta^{pm-2}|\nabla\eta|^2&\le\tfrac q4F_k(u)\eta^{\frac{pm-2}{\theta_1}}+C|\nabla\eta|^{\frac{2(q-\alpha)}{q+1}},\\
Cm^p\Psi_k(u)\eta^{p(m-1)}|\nabla\eta|^p&\le\tfrac q4F_k(u)\eta^{\frac{p(m-1)}{\theta_2}}+C|\nabla\eta|^{\frac{p(q-\alpha)}{q+p-1}}
\end{align*}
(if $\theta_i=0$ the corresponding bound holds without the first term). Condition \eqref{eq:m_sing} is equivalent to $\frac{pm-2}{\theta_1}\ge pm$ together with $\frac{p(m-1)}{\theta_2}\ge pm$, so both powers of $\eta$ are at most $\eta^{pm}$. The left-hand side of \eqref{eq:key} contains $\int g'(u)a_k(u)^2\eta^{pm}=q\int F_k(u)\eta^{pm}$, which is finite by \eqref{eq:stab_phi}. Absorbing half of it, we obtain
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^N}\Big(B'(H(\nabla u))H(\nabla u)|b_k'(u)|+F_k(u)\Big)\eta^{pm}\le C\int_{\Omega_1}|\nabla\eta|^{\frac{2(q-\alpha)}{q+1}}+C\int_{\Omega_2}|\nabla\eta|^{\frac{p(q-\alpha)}{q+p-1}}
\]
with $C$ independent of $k$. For each $t>0$ we have $F_k(t)=t^{\alpha-q}$ and $|b_k'(t)|=|\alpha|t^{\alpha-1}$ as soon as $k\ge1/t$. Fatou's lemma gives \eqref{eq:est_sing}.

so $\Phi_k/F_k^\theta$ and $\Psi_k/F_k^\theta$ are bounded by $C(1+\sigma)^{p}e^{-\frac{2\sigma}{\alpha+1}}\le C(p,\alpha)$ for $\sigma\ge0$.

We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:key} with $\psi=\eta^m$ and argue as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:est_sing}. Young's inequality with exponents $\frac{\alpha+1}\alpha$ and $\alpha+1$ produces the powers $|\nabla\eta|^{2(\alpha+1)}$ and $|\nabla\eta|^{p(\alpha+1)}$, and the powers of $\eta$ are at most $\eta^{pm}$ provided $pm\ge2(\alpha+1)$ and $m\ge\alpha+1$. Both hold since $m\ge\alpha+1$ and $p\ge2$. After absorption, $F_k(t)=e^{(\alpha+1)t}$ and $b_k'(t)=\alpha e^{\alpha t}$ as soon as $k>t$, and Fatou's lemma gives \eqref{eq:est_exp}.

label: lem:barrier
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:barrier}
Assume that $(H)$ holds and $p\ge2$. Let $\mathcal O\subset\mathbb{R}$ be an open interval and $h:\mathcal O\to(0,\infty)$ continuous and nonincreasing. Let $v\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}(E)\cap C(E)$ take values in $\mathcal O$ and satisfy $\Delta_p^Hv\le h(v)$ weakly in $E$, that is,
\[
\int_E\langle\mathcal A(\nabla v),\nabla\varphi\rangle\ge-\int_Eh(v)\varphi\qquad\text{for all }0\le\varphi\in C^1_c(E).
\]
For $r>R_0$ put $m(r):=\min_{\{H_0=r\}}v$, and for $R_1>R_0$ and $r,S>R_1$ put
\[
F(r):=\int_{R_1}^rs^{N-1}h(m(s))\,ds,\qquad \Lambda(S):=\int_{R_1}^S\big(r^{1-N}F(r)\big)^{\frac1{p-1}}dr,\qquad \mathcal L(S):=\int_{R_1}^Sr^{-\frac{N-1}{p-1}}dr .
\]
Then, for every $R_1>R_0$,
\[
\limsup_{S\to\infty}\frac{m(S)-\Lambda(S)}{\mathcal L(S)}<+\infty .
\]
head: environment

label: eq:ratio
title: Proof
body_md:
The function $m$ is continuous on $(R_0,\infty)$, since $v$ is uniformly continuous on compact subsets of $E$ and $m(r)=\min_{\{H_0=1\}}v(r\,\cdot)$. Put $f(r):=h(m(r))$, a continuous positive function. Fix $R_1>R_0$ and suppose, to reach a contradiction, that there are $S_j\to\infty$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ratio}
\frac{m(S_j)-\Lambda(S_j)}{\mathcal L(S_j)}\to+\infty .
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent\textit{The barriers.} For $S>R_1$ and $t\in\mathbb{R}$ let
\[
V_t(r):=m(R_1)+\int_{R_1}^r\varphi_p^{-1}\big(s^{1-N}(t+F(s))\big)ds,\qquad R_1\le r\le S .
\]
Then $V_t\in C^1([R_1,S])$, and $r^{N-1}\varphi_p(V_t'(r))=t+F(r)$ is of class $C^1$ with derivative $r^{N-1}f(r)$. The value $V_t(S)$ is a continuous and strictly increasing function of $t$ that tends to $\pm\infty$ as $t\to\pm\infty$. Let $t_S$ be the value for which $V_{t_S}(S)=m(S)$, and put $W(x):=V_{t_S}(H_0(x))$ on $A_S:=\{R_1<H_0<S\}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:radial}, $\Delta_p^HW=f(H_0(x))$ in $A_S$. Since $v\ge m(H_0(x))$ and $h$ is nonincreasing, $h(v(x))\le f(H_0(x))$, hence
\[
-\Delta_p^HW=-f(H_0)\le-h(v)\le-\Delta_p^Hv\qquad\text{weakly in }A_S .
\]
On $\{H_0=R_1\}$ we have $W=m(R_1)\le v$, and on $\{H_0=S\}$ we have $W=m(S)\le v$. Both right-hand sides are bounded on $\overline{A_S}$ because $v$ is continuous there. Lemma~\ref{lem:comparison} gives $W\le v$ in $A_S$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{The slopes.} Since $p\ge2$, $s\mapsto s^{\frac1{p-1}}$ is subadditive on $[0,\infty)$, and $\varphi_p^{-1}$ is increasing. With $t^+=\max\{t,0\}$ and $F\ge0$,
\[
V_t'(r)\le\varphi_p^{-1}\big(r^{1-N}(t^++F(r))\big)\le(t^+)^{\frac1{p-1}}r^{-\frac{N-1}{p-1}}+\big(r^{1-N}F(r)\big)^{\frac1{p-1}} .
\]
Integrating from $R_1$ to $S$ and using $V_{t_S}(S)=m(S)$, we get
\[
m(S)\le m(R_1)+(t_S^+)^{\frac1{p-1}}\mathcal L(S)+\Lambda(S).
\]
Since $\mathcal L(S)\ge\mathcal L(R_1+1)>0$ for $S\ge R_1+1$, \eqref{eq:ratio} gives $t_{S_j}\to+\infty$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Conclusion.} Fix $x_0$ with $H_0(x_0)=r_0:=R_1+1$. For $S_j>r_0$ with $t_{S_j}>0$, since $F\ge0$,
\[
v(x_0)\ge V_{t_{S_j}}(r_0)\ge m(R_1)+t_{S_j}^{\frac1{p-1}}\int_{R_1}^{r_0}r^{-\frac{N-1}{p-1}}dr\longrightarrow+\infty,
\]
which is absurd.

label: lem:decay_sing
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:decay_sing}
Assume that $(H)$ holds, $p\ge2$, $p\le N<\frac{p(p+3)}{p-1}$, and $q>q_c(N,p)$. Let $u$ be a positive weak solution of $\Delta_p^Hu=u^{-q}$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ that is stable outside a compact set $K$. Then $u$ is continuous in $\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K$ and
\[
\lim_{|x|\to\infty}|x|^{-\tau}u(x)=+\infty .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\beta:=\frac{N(q+p-1)}p$, so that $\frac N\beta=\tau$, and $\alpha_*:=q-\beta$. Then $\alpha_*\le1-p$ because $N\ge p$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:stable}(b), the assumption $q>q_c(N,p)$ means that $\alpha_0<1-p$ and $N(q+p-1)<p(q-\alpha_0)$, so $\alpha_*>\alpha_0$. For $\varepsilon\in(0,p)$ put $s_\varepsilon:=\frac N{p-\varepsilon}$ and $\alpha_\varepsilon:=q-s_\varepsilon(q+p-1)$. Then $\alpha_\varepsilon<\alpha_*$ and $\alpha_\varepsilon\to\alpha_*$ as $\varepsilon\to0$, and we fix $\varepsilon$ so small that $\alpha_\varepsilon>\alpha_0$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 1: continuity.} Write the equation as $\Delta_p^Hu=d(x)u^{p-1}$ with $d:=u^{-(q+p-1)}$, so that $d^{s_\varepsilon}=u^{\alpha_\varepsilon-q}$. For $\bar x\notin K$ and a ball $B_{2\rho}(\bar x)\subset\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K$, Proposition~\ref{prop:est_sing} with $\alpha=\alpha_\varepsilon$ and a cutoff function supported in $B_{2\rho}(\bar x)$ shows that $d\in L^{s_\varepsilon}(B_\rho(\bar x))$. Since $s_\varepsilon>\frac Np$, Lemma~\ref{lem:serrin}(i) shows that $u$ is locally bounded and continuous in $\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:serrin}(ii) shows that $u$ is locally bounded away from $0$ there.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 2: an integral bound at infinity.} Proposition~\ref{prop:est_sing} with $\alpha=\alpha_*$ and $\eta=\zeta_R$ gives, for $R>R_0+3$,
\[
\int_{B_R\setminus B_{R_0+2}}u^{-\beta}\le C\int_{B_{R_0+2}\setminus B_{R_0+1}}|\nabla\zeta_R|^{\frac{p(q-\alpha_*)}{q+p-1}}+C\int_{B_{2R}\setminus B_R}|\nabla\zeta_R|^{\frac{p(q-\alpha_*)}{q+p-1}}\le C+CR^{N-\frac{p\beta}{q+p-1}}=2C,
\]
since $\frac{p\beta}{q+p-1}=N$. Hence $u^{-\beta}\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus B_{R_0+2})$. If $p=N=2$, then $\alpha_*=-1$, which is allowed in Proposition~\ref{prop:est_sing}.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 3: a Harnack inequality at infinity.} Let $R\ge R_0+2$ and $|y|=8R$. Then $B_{4R}(y)\subset\{4R<|x|<12R\}$, so $u$ is stable in $B_{4R}(y)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:est_sing} with $\eta(x)=\eta_{2R}(x-y)$, which equals $1$ on $B_{2R}(y)$ and satisfies $|\nabla\eta|\le1/R$, gives
\[
\int_{B_{2R}(y)}u^{\alpha_\varepsilon-q}\le CR^{N-\frac{p(q-\alpha_\varepsilon)}{q+p-1}}=CR^{N-ps_\varepsilon},
\]
with $C$ independent of $R$ and $y$. Therefore
\[
R^{p-\frac N{s_\varepsilon}}\|d\|_{L^{s_\varepsilon}(B_{2R}(y))}=R^{\varepsilon}\Big(\int_{B_{2R}(y)}u^{\alpha_\varepsilon-q}\Big)^{\frac{p-\varepsilon}N}\le C,
\]
and Lemma~\ref{lem:serrin}(ii) gives $\sup_{B_R(y)}u\le K_*\inf_{B_R(y)}u$ with $K_*$ independent of $R$ and $y$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 4: conclusion.} Let $\vartheta>0$. By Step~2 there is $R_\vartheta\ge R_0+2$ with $\int_{\{|x|>R_\vartheta\}}u^{-\beta}\le\vartheta$. For $R\ge R_\vartheta$ and $|y|=8R$ we have $B_R(y)\subset\{|x|>7R\}$, so
\[
|B_1|R^N\Big(\sup_{B_R(y)}u\Big)^{-\beta}\le\int_{B_R(y)}u^{-\beta}\le\vartheta,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad\sup_{B_R(y)}u\ge\Big(\frac{|B_1|}\vartheta\Big)^{\frac1\beta}R^\tau .
\]
By Step~3, $u(y)\ge K_*^{-1}(|B_1|/\vartheta)^{1/\beta}(|y|/8)^\tau$ for $|y|\ge8R_\vartheta$. Since $\vartheta$ is arbitrary, the lemma follows.

label: lem:decay_exp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:decay_exp}
Assume that $(H)$ holds, $p\ge2$, and $p<N<\frac{p(p+3)}{p-1}$. Let $u$ be a weak solution of $-\Delta_p^Hu=e^u$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ that is stable outside a compact set $K$. Then $u$ is continuous in $\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K$ and
\[
\lim_{|x|\to\infty}|x|^pe^{u(x)}=0 .
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\alpha_*:=\frac Np-1$. The assumption on $N$ means exactly that $0<\alpha_*<\frac4{p-1}=\frac4\lambda$. Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,p)$ so small that $\alpha_\varepsilon:=\frac N{p-\varepsilon}-1<\frac4{p-1}$, and put $s_\varepsilon:=\alpha_\varepsilon+1=\frac N{p-\varepsilon}$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 1: continuity.} By Proposition~\ref{prop:est_exp} with $\alpha=\alpha_\varepsilon$ and cutoff functions supported in small balls, $e^u\in L^{s_\varepsilon}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K)$. Since $s_\varepsilon>\frac Np$, Lemma~\ref{lem:serrin}(i) shows that $u$ is locally bounded and continuous in $\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 2: an integral bound at infinity.} Proposition~\ref{prop:est_exp} with $\alpha=\alpha_*$, $m=\alpha_*+1$, and $\eta=\zeta_R$ gives
\[
\int_{B_R\setminus B_{R_0+2}}e^{\frac Npu}\le C+CR^{N-p(\alpha_*+1)}=2C,
\]
so $e^{\frac Npu}\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus B_{R_0+2})$.

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 3: a local maximum principle at infinity.} Let $\theta>0$ and $w:=e^{\theta u}$. Since $u$ is locally bounded in $\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K$, $w\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K)$ and $\nabla w=\theta w\nabla u$. By the homogeneity of $\mathcal A$, $\mathcal A(\nabla w)=\theta^{p-1}w^{p-1}\mathcal A(\nabla u)$. For $0\le\varphi\in C^1_c(\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K)$, the function $w^{p-1}\varphi$ is bounded, belongs to $W^{1,p}$, and has compact support, so it is admissible in the equation, and $\langle\mathcal A(\nabla u),\nabla u\rangle=H(\nabla u)^p\ge0$. Hence
\[
\int\langle\mathcal A(\nabla w),\nabla\varphi\rangle=\theta^{p-1}\int\langle\mathcal A(\nabla u),\nabla(w^{p-1}\varphi)\rangle-(p-1)\theta^p\int w^{p-1}H(\nabla u)^p\varphi\le\theta^{p-1}\int e^uw^{p-1}\varphi .
\]
That is, $-\Delta_p^Hw\le a(x)w^{p-1}$ with $a=\theta^{p-1}e^u$. Now take $\theta:=\frac N{p^2}$, so that $w^p=e^{\frac Npu}$. Let $R\ge R_0+2$ and $|y|=8R$. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:decay_sing}, Proposition~\ref{prop:est_exp} with $\alpha=\alpha_\varepsilon$ and $\eta(x)=\eta_{2R}(x-y)$ gives $\int_{B_{2R}(y)}e^{s_\varepsilon u}\le CR^{N-ps_\varepsilon}$, hence
\[
R^{p-\frac N{s_\varepsilon}}\|a\|_{L^{s_\varepsilon}(B_{2R}(y))}\le CR^{\varepsilon}\big(R^{N-ps_\varepsilon}\big)^{\frac{p-\varepsilon}N}=C .
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:serrin}(iii) gives $\sup_{B_R(y)}w\le K_*R^{-\frac Np}\|w\|_{L^p(B_{2R}(y))}$ with $K_*$ independent of $R$ and $y$. Since $w^{1/\theta}=e^u$, this reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:locmax}
\sup_{B_R(y)}e^u\le K_*^{\frac1\theta}R^{-p}\Big(\int_{B_{2R}(y)}e^{\frac Npu}\Big)^{\frac pN}.
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 4: conclusion.} Let $\vartheta>0$ and choose $R_\vartheta\ge R_0+2$ with $\int_{\{|x|>R_\vartheta\}}e^{\frac Npu}\le\vartheta$. For $|y|\ge8R_\vartheta$ let $R=|y|/8$. Then $B_{2R}(y)\subset\{|x|>6R\}$, and \eqref{eq:locmax} gives $|y|^pe^{u(y)}\le8^pK_*^{1/\theta}\vartheta^{p/N}$. Since $\vartheta$ is arbitrary, the lemma follows.

title: Proof

Put $w_j:=(1+s_j)^{N-2}$. For $N=2$, $w_j=1$. Then $\eta$ is Lipschitz with compact support in $\{|x|>2^{j_0-1}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^N\setminus K$, and $|\nabla\eta|\le c_j/(|x|\log2)$ on $A_j$ for $J\le j<J'$. The stability inequality, which holds for such $\eta$ by the density argument of Step~1 in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:key}, together with \eqref{eq:MN} and Lemma~\ref{lem:annulus}, gives
\[

\[
\sum_{j=j_0}^{J-1}\mu_j\le D_0+C\Big(\sum_{j=J}^{J'-1}w_j^{-1}\Big)^{-1}\qquad(j_0<J<J').

\[

\[

\medskip\noindent\textit{Step 1: $X>L$ on $\mathbb{R}$.} Suppose not, and let $s_0$ be the first point with $X(s_0)=L$. On $(-\infty,s_0)$ we have $X>L$, hence $\big(e^{(N-q\tau)s}Y\big)'<e^{(N-q\tau)s}L^{-q}$. Integrating from $-\infty$ gives $Y<(\tau L)^{p-1}$ on $(-\infty,s_0]$, and therefore $X'=Y^{1/(p-1)}-\tau X<0$ there, including at $s_0$. So $X$ decreases strictly from $+\infty$ to $L$ on $(-\infty,s_0]$, and we can write $X'=h(X)$ with $h\in C^1([L,\infty))$ and $h<0$. Differentiating $X'=Y^{1/(p-1)}-\tau X$ and using the equation for $Y$, we find that
\[
h(\xi)h'(\xi)=-\tau h(\xi)+\frac1{p-1}\big(h(\xi)+\tau\xi\big)^{2-p}\xi^{-q}-\frac{N-q\tau}{p-1}\big(h(\xi)+\tau\xi\big),\qquad \xi\ge L,
\]
where $h(\xi)+\tau\xi=Y^{1/(p-1)}>0$, and $h(\xi)+\tau\xi\to0$ as $\xi\to\infty$.

Fix $\mu>\tau$. The function $\xi\mapsto h(\xi)-\mu(L-\xi)$ is negative at $\xi=L$ and equals $(\mu-\tau)\xi-\mu L+o(1)$ as $\xi\to\infty$. Let $\xi_\mu>L$ be its smallest zero. Then $h'(\xi_\mu)\ge-\mu$, and with $\sigma:=\xi_\mu-L>0$ we have $h(\xi_\mu)=-\mu\sigma$ and $h(\xi_\mu)+\tau\xi_\mu=\tau L-(\mu-\tau)\sigma>0$. Put
\[

\]
Both $\log(\tau L-(\mu-\tau)t)^{2-p}$ and $\log(L+t)^{-q}$ are convex, the second strictly, so $\Phi$ is strictly convex and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi}
\Phi(\sigma)>\Phi(0)+\Phi'(0)\sigma=(N-q\tau)\tau L+(N-q\tau)\big[(p-2)(\mu-\tau)-q\tau\big]\sigma,
\end{equation}
where we used $L^{-q}=(N-q\tau)(\tau L)^{p-1}$. Dividing the equation for $h$ at $\xi_\mu$ by $h(\xi_\mu)=-\mu\sigma<0$ and using \eqref{eq:Phi}, we obtain
\[
h'(\xi_\mu)=-\tau-\frac{\Phi(\sigma)}{(p-1)\mu\sigma}+\frac{(N-q\tau)\big(\tau L-(\mu-\tau)\sigma\big)}{(p-1)\mu\sigma}<-\tau+\frac{N-q\tau}{(p-1)\mu}\big[q\tau-(p-1)(\mu-\tau)\big].
\]
Combining this with $h'(\xi_\mu)\ge-\mu$, multiplying by $(p-1)\mu$, and using $\tau(q+p-1)=p$, we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quad}
\mu^2-\big[N-(q-1)\tau\big]\mu+\frac{p}{p-1}(N-q\tau)>0\qquad\text{for every }\mu>\tau .
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:zcond}, the left-hand side has real roots $\mu_-\le\mu_+$. Since $N-(q+1)\tau>0$, the inequality $\mu_->\tau$ is equivalent to $\big(N-(q+1)\tau\big)^2>D$, that is, to $-4\tau(N-q\tau)>-\frac{4p}{p-1}(N-q\tau)$, which holds because $\tau<\frac p{p-1}$.
